dryRun.title: Running median of the stream 5, 2, 8, 1  (low = max-heap of the smaller half, high = min-heap of the bigger half)
dryRun.note: The two heaps meet in the middle: the top of low is the biggest of the small half, the top of high is the smallest of the big half. The median is always one of these two tops, or their average.

think.q:
const low = [1, 2]      // the smaller half
const high = [5, 8]     // the bigger half
console.log((Math.max(...low) + Math.min(...high)) / 2)
why: With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values: the biggest of the small half (2) and the smallest of the big half (5). That is 3.5.
The heaps give both of these in O(1), because they sit at the roots.
think.exec:
const low = [1, 2]      // the smaller half
const high = [5, 8]     // the bigger half
console.log((Math.max(...low) + Math.min(...high)) / 2)

think.q: Which two rules must always hold for the two heaps?
opts: Both heaps have the same items
Every item in low is at most every item in high, and their sizes differ by at most 1
low is sorted and high is not
low holds odd numbers and high holds even numbers
why: The first rule says the halves are really a split of the sorted order. The second rule puts the median at the roots.
After each insert you may have to move one item from one heap to the other to restore the sizes.

think.q: Why is the smaller half stored in a max-heap?
opts: Because it is easier to write
Because we need its biggest item, the one closest to the middle, at the root
why: The median sits between the halves, so we need the largest of the small half and the smallest of the big half.
That is a max-heap for the small half and a min-heap for the big half.

think.q: A median finder takes n numbers one at a time. What are the cost of add and the cost of median?
why: An add pushes into a heap and maybe moves one item: a few O(log n) steps. The median is just a look at the roots.
Keeping one sorted array makes each add O(n), because items have to shift.

think.q: You keep low one item bigger than high when the count is odd. Where is the median?
why: The bigger heap holds the extra middle item, so its root is the median.
Pick one convention (low gets the extra) and keep to it everywhere.

try.task: Write createMedianFinder(). It returns an object with add(x) and median(). median() returns the median of all numbers added so far (the average of the two middle numbers when the count is even), or undefined if nothing was added. 100,000 adds must be fast.
try.hint: Write a small heap helper that takes a compare function. Use low as a max-heap and high as a min-heap. Add to low, move its top to high, then if high is bigger than low, move one back.

checks.verify: const m = createMedianFinder(); m.add(1); const a = m.median(); m.add(2); const b = m.median(); m.add(3); const d = m.median(); assert(a === 1 && b === 1.5 && d === 2, "expected 1, 1.5, 2 but got " + a + ", " + b + ", " + d)
const m = createMedianFinder(); const out = []; for (const x of [5, 2, 8, 1]) { m.add(x); out.push(m.median()) } assert(JSON.stringify(out) === "[5,3.5,5,3.5]", "got " + JSON.stringify(out))
const m = createMedianFinder(); for (const x of [-1, -1, 4, 4]) m.add(x); assert(m.median() === 1.5, "expected 1.5, got " + m.median())

const m = createMedianFinder(); const t0 = Date.now(); for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) m.add((i * 7919) % 100003); assert(m.median() === 49999.5 && Date.now() - t0 < 1500, "wrong median or too slow, add must be O(log n)")

takeaway.key: Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the bigger half in a min-heap, sizes within 1. The median is at the roots: add O(log n), median O(1).
mistakes: Forgetting to rebalance after an add, so the sizes drift apart.
Putting a bigger item in the small half.
Returning the wrong root when the count is odd.
Keeping one sorted array (add costs O(n)).

dryRun.title: Merge [[1, 3], [8, 10], [2, 6], [15, 18]]. First sort by start: [1,3] [2,6] [8,10] [15,18]
dryRun.note: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the last merged one. If it does, stretch the end with max. If not, it starts a new group.

think.q:
const iv = [[8, 10], [1, 3], [2, 6]]
iv.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0])
console.log(JSON.stringify(iv))
why: The compare function looks at the start (a[0]). Without it, sort would compare the arrays as strings.
Sorting by start is what makes one pass enough.
think.exec:
const iv = [[8, 10], [1, 3], [2, 6]]
iv.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0])
console.log(JSON.stringify(iv))

think.q:
const overlap = (a, b) => a[1] >= b[0]
console.log(overlap([1, 4], [4, 5]))

For "merge intervals", do [1, 4] and [4, 5] count as overlapping?
why: They share the point 4, so they merge into [1, 5]. Whether touching counts is a detail you must ask about: here it does (>=).
For "meeting rooms" the usual answer is the opposite: a meeting ending at 4 and another starting at 4 do not clash.
think.exec:
const overlap = (a, b) => a[1] >= b[0]
console.log(overlap([1, 4], [4, 5]))

think.q:
const iv = [[1, 10], [2, 3]]
const out = [iv[0].slice()]
for (const cur of iv.slice(1)) {
  const last = out[out.length - 1]
  if (cur[0] <= last[1]) last[1] = cur[1]
  else out.push(cur.slice())
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(out))

The correct answer is [[1,10]]. What does this print?
why: last[1] = cur[1] shrinks the end from 10 to 3, because the new interval sits inside the old one.
Always extend with Math.max(last[1], cur[1]).

think.q: What is the time of the merge-intervals solution?
why: Sorting costs O(n log n). The merge pass after it is a single O(n) loop, so sorting dominates.
If the input is already sorted by start, the whole thing is O(n).

think.q: "Can one person attend all of these meetings?" With the meetings sorted by start, what do you check?
opts: That the total length is under 24 hours
That each meeting starts at or after the previous one ends
That no two meetings have the same length
That the list has an even size
why: After sorting, a clash can only happen between neighbours. One pass comparing start[i] with end[i-1] decides it.
"How many rooms are needed?" is the next level: a min-heap of end times.

try.task: Write mergeIntervals(intervals). Each interval is [start, end]. Merge all intervals that overlap or touch, and return the result sorted by start. Do not change the input.
try.hint: Copy and sort by start. Keep an output list. For each interval, compare its start with the end of the last output interval: if start <= lastEnd, set lastEnd = Math.max(lastEnd, end), otherwise push it.

checks.verify: const x = [[2, 6], [1, 3]]; mergeIntervals(x); assert(JSON.stringify(x) === "[[2,6],[1,3]]", "the input was changed")

takeaway.key: Sort by start, then one pass: if the next interval starts at or before the last end, extend the end with max; otherwise start a new one. O(n log n).
mistakes: Not sorting first.
Setting the end to the new end instead of the max of both.
Deciding wrongly whether touching intervals merge.
Changing the caller's arrays.

dryRun.title: Pick the most non-overlapping intervals from [1,3] [2,4] [3,5] [0,6] [5,7] [8,9] [5,9], sorted by END time
dryRun.note: Greedy = make the locally best choice and never look back. Here "best" means the interval that ends first, because it leaves the most room for the rest.

think.q:
const iv = [[1, 3], [2, 4], [3, 5], [0, 6], [5, 7], [8, 9], [5, 9]]
iv.sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1])
let end = -Infinity, count = 0
for (const [s, e] of iv) {
  if (s >= end) { count++; end = e }
}
console.log(count)
why: Sorted by end, the code takes [1,3], [3,5], [5,7] and [8,9]. That is 4 intervals that never overlap.
The only decision per interval is "does it start after my last chosen end?".

think.q:
const iv = [[0, 10], [1, 2], [3, 4]]
iv.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0])   // sorted by START
let end = -Infinity, count = 0
for (const [s, e] of iv) {
  if (s >= end) { count++; end = e }
}
console.log(count)

The best answer is 2 ([1,2] and [3,4]). What does this version print?
why: Sorting by start takes the huge [0,10] first and blocks everything else, so the answer is 1.
The idea of "take the earliest" is only right when you choose the right measure: earliest end, not earliest start.

think.q:
function canJump(nums) {
  let reach = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (i > reach) return false
    reach = Math.max(reach, i + nums[i])
  }
  return true
}
console.log(canJump([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]), canJump([3, 2, 1, 0, 4]))
why: In the first array you can always push the reach forward to the end. In the second, every path ends on the 0 at index 3, so index 4 is out of reach.
The greedy idea: you never need to remember paths, only the furthest index you can reach.

think.q:
const coins = [4, 3, 1]
let left = 6, used = 0
for (const c of coins) {
  used += Math.floor(left / c)
  left %= c
}
console.log(used)

The fewest coins for 6 is 2 (3 + 3). What does "always take the biggest coin" give?
why: It takes 4, then 1, then 1: three coins. The locally best choice (the biggest coin) blocks the better answer.
When greedy fails like this, you need dynamic programming. Always test a greedy idea on a small counter-example.
think.exec:
const coins = [4, 3, 1]
let left = 6, used = 0
for (const c of coins) {
  used += Math.floor(left / c)
  left %= c
}
console.log(used)

think.q: How do you convince yourself (and the interviewer) that a greedy choice is correct?
opts: You argue that swapping any optimal answer's first choice for the greedy choice never makes it worse (an exchange argument), and you try a small counter-example
why: Examples can pass by luck. A short argument that "my choice is at least as good as any other first choice" is the real proof.
Say it in words: "taking the earliest end leaves the most room for the others".

try.task: Write maxMeetings(intervals). Each meeting is [start, end]. Return the largest number of meetings one person can attend. A meeting may start exactly when another one ends.
try.hint: Sort a copy by end. Keep lastEnd = -Infinity. Take a meeting when start >= lastEnd and then set lastEnd to its end.

checks.t: one long meeting hides two short ones
empty input and does not change the input
checks.verify: const x = [[3, 4], [1, 2]]; maxMeetings(x); assert(maxMeetings([]) === 0 && JSON.stringify(x) === "[[3,4],[1,2]]", "edge cases")

takeaway.key: Greedy = take the locally best choice and never undo it. It needs the right sort or measure (for intervals: earliest end) and a reason it is safe. If a small counter-example breaks it, use DP.
mistakes: Sorting by start when the rule needs earliest end.
Trusting a greedy idea without trying a counter-example (coins 4, 3, 1).
Using > instead of >= and rejecting meetings that only touch.
Changing the input array while sorting.

dryRun.title: Build an adjacency list for 4 nodes and the edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 2-3 (undirected)
rows: 1 to the list of 0, and 0 to the list of 1
2 to the list of 0, and 0 to the list of 2
2 to the list of 1, and 1 to the list of 2
3 to the list of 2, and 2 to the list of 3
dryRun.note: An undirected edge is written twice, once in each direction. A directed edge is written once. The list answers "who are my neighbours?" quickly.

think.q:
const n = 4
const edges = [[0, 1], [0, 2], [1, 2], [2, 3]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => [])
for (const [a, b] of edges) {
  adj[a].push(b)
  adj[b].push(a)
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(adj))
why: Each edge is pushed in both directions, so node 2 knows 0, 1 and 3. Its list length (3) is its degree.
The index in the outer array is the node, and the inner array holds its neighbours.

think.q:
const edges = [[0, 1], [0, 2], [1, 2], [2, 3]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: 4 }, () => [])
for (const [a, b] of edges) adj[a].push(b)
console.log(JSON.stringify(adj))
why: For a directed graph each edge is stored once, from a to b. Node 3 has no outgoing edge, so its list is empty.
Read the problem: "undirected" means push both ways.

think.q:
const adj = new Array(3).fill([])
adj[0].push(1)
console.log(adj[2].length)
why: fill([]) puts the same array in all three slots, so the push shows up in every node.
Use Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) to get a fresh list per node.

think.q: A graph has V nodes and E edges. How much space do an adjacency list and an adjacency matrix use?
why: The list stores each edge once or twice. The matrix stores a cell for every pair of nodes, even when there are few edges.
Use a matrix only for small, dense graphs.

think.q: You often ask "is there an edge between a and b?". What do the two forms cost?
opts: Matrix O(1), list O(degree of a)
why: The matrix looks at one cell. The list may scan all neighbours of a. If it matters, keep a Set of neighbours per node.
For "visit all neighbours", the list is faster: it never touches non-edges.

try.task: Write buildGraph(n, edges, directed). Nodes are numbered 0 to n - 1. edges is a list of [a, b]. Return an adjacency list: an array of n arrays, where the array at index i holds the neighbours of i in the order the edges were given. If directed is false, store each edge both ways.
try.hint: Start with Array.from({ length: n }, () => []). For each [a, b] push b into adj[a], and if not directed, push a into adj[b].

checks.t: every node gets its own list
checks.verify: const g = buildGraph(3, [[0, 1]], true); g[2].push(9); assert(g[1].length === 0 && g[0].length === 1, "the lists share the same array")

checks.t: a self-loop and repeated edges are kept as given

takeaway.key: Use an adjacency list: one array of neighbours per node, O(V + E) space. Push each undirected edge both ways. Create the inner arrays separately.
mistakes: new Array(n).fill([]), which shares one list.
Pushing an undirected edge only one way.
Using a matrix for a big, sparse graph.
Mixing 0-based and 1-based node numbers.

dryRun.title: BFS from node 0 on a square: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3
dryRun.note: Mark a node as seen when you put it in the queue, not when you take it out. Otherwise the same node can enter the queue twice. The first time BFS reaches a node is the shortest way there.

think.q:
const adj = [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0, 3], [1, 2]]
const dist = Array(4).fill(-1)
dist[0] = 0
const q = [0]
while (q.length) {
  const u = q.shift()
  for (const v of adj[u]) {
    if (dist[v] === -1) {
      dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
      q.push(v)
    }
  }
}
console.log(dist.join(","))
why: Nodes 1 and 2 are one step from 0. Node 3 is two steps away through either of them.
dist[v] === -1 doubles as the "not seen yet" check, so no separate visited array is needed.

think.q:
const adj = [[1], [0], [3], [2]]
const seen = new Set([0])
const q = [0]
while (q.length) {
  const u = q.shift()
  for (const v of adj[u]) {
    if (!seen.has(v)) { seen.add(v); q.push(v) }
  }
}
console.log(seen.size)
why: The graph has two separate pieces: {0, 1} and {2, 3}. BFS from 0 can only reach its own piece.
To visit a whole disconnected graph, start a new BFS from every node that is still unseen.

think.q: Why do we mark a node as seen when it enters the queue, and not when it leaves?
opts: Otherwise the same node can be queued many times by different neighbours, wasting time and breaking distance counts
why: If node 3 is reached from both 1 and 2 before it is popped, marking late would push it twice.
Mark early, and each node is queued exactly once.

think.q: In which graphs does BFS give the shortest path (fewest edges)?
opts: Any graph where every edge counts the same (unweighted)
why: BFS reaches nodes in rings of distance 1, 2, 3, and so on. The first arrival is therefore the shortest.
With different edge weights you need Dijkstra instead.

think.q: What is the time of BFS on a graph with V nodes and E edges (adjacency list)?
why: Each node is queued once and each edge is looked at once (twice if undirected).
With an adjacency matrix it becomes O(V²), because every row must be scanned.

try.task: Write shortestPath(n, edges, start, end). The graph is undirected with nodes 0 to n - 1. Return the fewest edges on a path from start to end, or -1 if there is no path. If start === end return 0.
try.hint: Build the adjacency list, then run BFS from start keeping a dist array filled with -1. Return dist[end].

checks.t: the short way wins over the long way

checks.verify: const n = 100000; const e = Array.from({ length: n - 1 }, (_, i) => [i, i + 1]); const t0 = Date.now(); assert(shortestPath(n, e, 0, n - 1) === n - 1 && Date.now() - t0 < 1000, "wrong or too slow, avoid queue.shift on a huge array")

takeaway.key: BFS on a graph: a queue, a seen/dist marker set when queued, and the first arrival is the shortest path in an unweighted graph. O(V + E). Restart from unseen nodes to cover all components.
mistakes: Marking nodes as seen only when popped.
Using BFS for weighted edges.
Forgetting that BFS from one node only covers its component.
Calling shift() on a very large array in a hot loop (use level arrays or an index).

dryRun.title: Count the connected components of 6 nodes with edges 0-1, 1-2, 3-4
dryRun.note: Loop over all nodes. Whenever you meet a node that is not seen, it starts a new component: count it, then DFS to mark everything connected to it.

think.q:
const n = 6, edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4]]
const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => [])
for (const [a, b] of edges) { adj[a].push(b); adj[b].push(a) }
const seen = new Array(n).fill(false)
const dfs = (u) => {
  seen[u] = true
  for (const v of adj[u]) if (!seen[v]) dfs(v)
}
let count = 0
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  if (!seen[i]) { count++; dfs(i) }
}
console.log(count)
why: The groups are {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4} and {5}. A node with no edges is its own component.
Each time the loop finds an unseen node, a whole new group starts.

think.q:
const adj = [[1, 2], [3], [3], []]
const order = []
const seen = new Set()
function dfs(u) {
  seen.add(u)
  order.push(u)
  for (const v of adj[u]) if (!seen.has(v)) dfs(v)
}
dfs(0)
console.log(order.join(","))
why: From 0 it goes to its first neighbour 1, then straight on to 3 (depth first), and only then comes back to try 2.
BFS would give 0,1,2,3 instead. The difference is "go deep first" versus "go wide first".

think.q: In an undirected graph, you find a cycle if DFS reaches a seen node. Which neighbour must you skip?
opts: The node you just came from (the parent)
why: In an undirected graph, an edge a-b appears in both lists. Going from a to b and then seeing a again is not a cycle.
A seen node that is not the parent proves a real cycle. (For directed graphs you track the current path instead.)

think.q: A graph is a chain of 100,000 nodes. What can go wrong with a recursive DFS?
opts: The call stack overflows, so use an explicit stack or BFS
why: The recursion goes 100,000 calls deep, far past what JavaScript allows (about ten thousand).
An iterative DFS with your own stack, or a BFS, avoids the problem.

think.q: What is the time of DFS over a whole graph with V nodes and E edges?
why: Each node is marked once and each edge is checked once or twice.
The extra space is O(V) for the seen markers plus the stack depth.

try.task: Write countComponents(n, edges). The graph is undirected with nodes 0 to n - 1. Return how many connected components it has (a node alone counts as one). It must work for a chain of 50,000 nodes.
try.hint: Build the adjacency list. Loop over all nodes: if one is unseen, add 1 and mark everything it reaches. Use your own stack (an array with push and pop) instead of recursion.

checks.t: a cycle does not add components
a chain of 50,000 nodes (recursion would crash)
checks.verify: const n = 50000; const e = Array.from({ length: n - 1 }, (_, i) => [i, i + 1]); assert(countComponents(n, e) === 1, "expected 1, did you use deep recursion?")

takeaway.key: DFS goes deep along one path before trying others. Loop over all nodes and start a DFS from each unseen one to count components. O(V + E). For very long chains use an explicit stack.
mistakes: Not marking a node as seen before exploring it.
Treating the parent as a cycle in an undirected graph.
Deep recursion on huge chains.
Forgetting nodes that have no edges.

flags: two-heaps: the try-it reference solution has its own small heap builder; the 100,000 add check compares the exact final median (computed in the generator).
greedy: the lesson shows the failing coin greedy on purpose as a warning, and no knapsack/coin DP is taught here (that is in the DP unit).
bfs-graphs: the long-chain check forbids a slow queue.shift pattern; the reference uses level arrays.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
